Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) can paradoxically reduce BBB penetration due to excessive plasma protein binding and poor aqueous solubility, which reduce the free fraction available for diffusion.

(A) does not cross the BBB (B) crosses the BBB

Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) can paradoxically reduce BBB penetration due to excessive plasma protein binding and poor aqueous solubility, which reduce the free fraction available for diffusion.

Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) can paradoxically reduce BBB penetration due to excessive plasma protein binding and poor aqueous solubility, which reduce the free fraction available for diffusion.

Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) can paradoxically reduce BBB penetration due to excessive plasma protein binding and poor aqueous solubility, which reduce the free fraction available for diffusion.

Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) can paradoxically reduce BBB penetration due to excessive plasma protein binding and poor aqueous solubility, which reduce the free fraction available for diffusion.

Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) can paradoxically reduce BBB penetration due to excessive plasma protein binding and poor aqueous solubility, which reduce the free fraction available for diffusion.

Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) can paradoxically reduce BBB penetration due to excessive plasma protein binding and poor aqueous solubility, which reduce the free fraction available for diffusion.

Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) can paradoxically reduce BBB penetration due to excessive plasma protein binding and poor aqueous solubility, which reduce the free fraction available for diffusion.

Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) can paradoxically reduce BBB penetration due to excessive plasma protein binding and poor aqueous solubility, which reduce the free fraction available for diffusion.

Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) can paradoxically reduce BBB penetration due to excessive plasma protein binding and poor aqueous solubility, which reduce the free fraction available for diffusion.

Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) can paradoxically reduce BBB penetration due to excessive plasma protein binding and poor aqueous solubility, which reduce the free fraction available for diffusion.

Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) can paradoxically reduce BBB penetration due to excessive plasma protein binding and poor aqueous solubility, which reduce the free fraction available for diffusion.

Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) can paradoxically reduce BBB penetration due to excessive plasma protein binding and poor aqueous solubility, which reduce the free fraction available for diffusion.

Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) can paradoxically reduce BBB penetration due to excessive plasma protein binding and poor aqueous solubility, which reduce the free fraction available for diffusion.

Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) can paradoxically reduce BBB penetration due to excessive plasma protein binding and poor aqueous solubility, which reduce the free fraction available for diffusion.

Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells connected by tight junctions, surrounded by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Unlike peripheral capillaries, the BBB has no fenestrations and minimal pinocytosis, so drug entry into the CNS requires either passive transcellular diffusion through the endothelial cell membranes or carrier-mediated transport. Efflux transporters — particularly P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) — on the luminal side actively pump many compounds back into the blood, creating an additional barrier beyond simple membrane permeability.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 70-80 Å²) is the strongest single predictor of BBB penetration — the tight junctions eliminate the paracellular route, so transcellular diffusion is the only passive pathway. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 1-2) — more restrictive than for intestinal absorption because the BBB endothelium is less permeable. Small to moderate molecular weight (MW < 450 Da). Low overall hydrogen bonding capacity. Most successful CNS drugs are small, moderately lipophilic, and have minimal polar surface area. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da).
